title: 2020_PMC7006828_Kansan_Guardian_Perceptions_of_HPV_and_the_HPV_Vaccine_and_the_R
ehr_evidence: From January 31 - March 21, 2017, data were collected via an online survey.
summary: A cross-sectional online survey of Kansas guardians of children aged 9-17 years (n=95) assessing perceptions of HPV and the HPV vaccine, social media exposure, and their influence on vaccination decisions.
key_findings: Of 95 eligible participants, 55 (57.9%) indicated seeing information about HPV and the HPV vaccine on social media.

Children of guardians with annual household income of $100,000 or more were significantly more likely to have received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine compared to children of guardians earning under $100,000 (p = 0.003).

Participants who had seen information on social media about the HPV vaccine (M = 2.50, SD = 1.62) were significantly more likely to perceive that the HPV vaccine could kill their child than those who had not seen information (M = 1.74, SD = 0.85; t(79) = 0.019).

Higher scores on the HPV vaccine harm perception scale (β = -0.451) significantly predicted lower scores on the HPV vaccine effectiveness perception scale, explaining 38.5% of the variance (R = 0.620; F[1, 57] = 35.63; p < 0.0001).
Region had a significant effect on perception of HPV vaccine inconvenience for children (F[6, 80) = 2.96; p = 0.012).
Participants perceived their fears about getting their child the HPV vaccine were neither significantly increased nor decreased by social media (M = 0.11, SD = 0.50; t(54) = 1.63, p = 0.109).
No significant differences were found between groups on HPV-related items when comparing those who had or had not seen information on social media.
captured_features: guardian demographics (sex, guardian identity, age/generation, race, ethnicity, education, annual household income, region of residence)
HPV and HPV vaccine perceptions (health belief model and social amplification of risk scales)
perceptions of social media messages about HPV and HPV vaccine
pathologies_diseases: HPV-related cancers (cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal, oropharyngeal)
population: Kansas guardians of children aged 9-17 years (n = 95 eligible online survey participants; 87.4% female, 87.4% mothers, predominantly White, non-Hispanic)
exposure_domain: social media messages about HPV and the HPV vaccine
limitations: Convenience sample with limited representativeness and small sample size (n = 95).
Self-reported data with potential recall and social desirability bias.
Low survey completion rate (41.6% of those who began the survey).
